Express $2\sin 17^{∘}\cos 17^{∘}$ as a single trigonometric ratio.

Simplify $$
\displaystyle {\left(\operatorname{sin}\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)+\operatorname{cos}\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)\right)}^{2}.
$$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
First, we expand the parenthesis and use the Pythagorean identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\left(\operatorname{sin}\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)+\operatorname{cos}\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)\right)}^{2} & ={sin}^{2}\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)+2\operatorname{sin}\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)\operatorname{cos}\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)+{cos}^{2}\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right) \\  & =\left[{sin}^{2}\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)+{cos}^{2}\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)\right]+2\operatorname{sin}\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)\operatorname{cos}\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right) \\  & =1+2\operatorname{sin}\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)\operatorname{cos}\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's recall the double-angle formula for sine: 

$$
2\operatorname{sin}x\operatorname{cos}x=\operatorname{sin}2x
$$

Substituting $x=\frac{\pi }{6}$ into the above, we get

$$
2\operatorname{sin}\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)\operatorname{cos}\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)=\operatorname{sin}\left(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{6}\right)=\operatorname{sin}\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right).
$$

Therefore,

$$
{\left(\operatorname{sin}\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)+\operatorname{cos}\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)\right)}^{2}=1+2\operatorname{sin}\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)\operatorname{cos}\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)=1+\operatorname{sin}\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right).
$$

questions.:question/problem:

\displaystyle 6\operatorname{sin}\left(\frac{3\pi }{10}\right)\operatorname{cos}\left(\frac{3\pi }{10}\right)
$$ as a single trigonometric ratio.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
First, let's recall the double-angle formula for sine: 

$$
2\operatorname{sin}x\operatorname{cos}x=\operatorname{sin}2x
$$

Substituting $x=\frac{3\pi }{10}$ into the above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}\left(\frac{3\pi }{10}\right)\operatorname{cos}\left(\frac{3\pi }{10}\right) & =\operatorname{sin}\left(2\cdot \frac{3\pi }{10}\right)=\operatorname{sin}\left(\frac{3\pi }{5}\right).\end{aligned}

Therefore, 

$$
6\operatorname{sin}\left(\frac{3\pi }{10}\right)\operatorname{cos}\left(\frac{3\pi }{10}\right)=3\cdot 2\operatorname{sin}\left(\frac{3\pi }{10}\right)\operatorname{cos}\left(\frac{3\pi }{10}\right)=3\operatorname{sin}\left(\frac{3\pi }{5}\right).

questions.:question/problem:
Simplify the expression. Choose an equivalent expression involving the sine of twice the given angle.

$$
\left(\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{7}\right)-\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{7}\right)\right)^2.
$$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Put $x=\frac{\pi}{7}$. First, expand the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}
(\sin x-\cos x)^2
&=\sin^2 x-2\sin x\cos x+\cos^2 x\\
&=(\sin^2 x+\cos^2 x)-2\sin x\cos x\\
&=1-2\sin x\cos x.
\end{aligned}
$$

Here we used $\sin^2 x+\cos^2 x=1$. Now apply the double-angle formula $2\sin x\cos x=\sin(2x)$:

$$
(\sin x-\cos x)^2=1-\sin(2x).
$$

Substituting $x=\frac{\pi}{7}$ gives the result

$$
1-\sin\left(2\cdot\frac{\pi}{7}\right)=1-\sin\left(\frac{2\pi}{7}\right).
$$

The cross term is negative because the original binomial is a difference.

questions.:question/problem: Express $2\sin 23^\circ\cos 23^\circ$ as a single trigonometric ratio.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Recall the double-angle formula for sine:

$$
2\sin x\cos x=\sin(2x).
$$

Substituting $x=23^\circ$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
2\sin 23^\circ\cos 23^\circ
&=\sin(2\cdot23^\circ)\\
&=\sin 46^\circ.
\end{aligned}
$$

The angle doubles; the factor $2$ is already included in the identity.

questions.:question/problem:
Express the following as a constant multiple of a single trigonometric ratio.

$$
\sin^3\left(\frac{\pi}{11}\right)\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{11}\right)
+\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{11}\right)\cos^3\left(\frac{\pi}{11}\right).
$$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Factor out the common product $\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{11}\right)\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{11}\right)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\sin^3\left(\frac{\pi}{11}\right)\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{11}\right)+\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{11}\right)\cos^3\left(\frac{\pi}{11}\right)\\
&\quad=\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{11}\right)\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{11}\right)
\left(\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi}{11}\right)+\cos^2\left(\frac{\pi}{11}\right)\right)\\
&\quad=\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{11}\right)\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{11}\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

The parenthesis equals $1$ by the Pythagorean identity. Recall that $2\sin x\cos x=\sin(2x)$, so a product without the factor $2$ is half the corresponding sine:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{11}\right)\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{11}\right)
&=\frac{1}{2}\left[2\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{11}\right)\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{11}\right)\right]\\
&=\frac{1}{2}\sin\left(\frac{2\pi}{11}\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

questions.:question/problem:
Express the following as a constant multiple of a single trigonometric ratio.

$$
-4\sin\left(11^\circ\right)\cos\left(11^\circ\right)
$$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Put $x=11^\circ$. Recall $2\sin x\cos x=\sin(2x)$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
-4\sin x\cos x &=-2\left[2\sin x\cos x\right] \\ &=-2\sin(2x)
\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute $x=11^\circ$ and double the whole angle: $2x=22^\circ$. The result is

$$
-2\sin\left(22^\circ\right) .
$$

$$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Put $x=28^\circ$. Expand the square and combine the squared terms.

$$

questions.:question/problem:
Simplify to a constant multiple of a single trigonometric ratio.

$$
\frac{\frac{1}{2}\sin\left(11^\circ\right)\cos\left(11^\circ\right)}{\cos\left(22^\circ\right)}
$$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Put $x=11^\circ$. Recall $2\sin x\cos x=\sin(2x)$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\frac{1}{2}\sin x\cos x}{\cos(2x)} &=\frac{1}{4}\frac{2\sin x\cos x}{\cos(2x)} \\ &=\frac{1}{4}\frac{\sin(2x)}{\cos(2x)} \\ &=\frac{1}{4}\tan(2x)
\end{aligned}
$$

The denominator is nonzero, and $\tan(2x)=\sin(2x)/\cos(2x)$.

Substitute $x=11^\circ$ and double the whole angle: $2x=22^\circ$. The result is

$$
\frac{1}{4}\tan\left(22^\circ\right) .
$$
